b: Before my brother Jonathan died, I told him about the plans Joey and I were considering. We were thinking about moving to the Philippines, selling our house in Boca Raton, Florida, and renting instead of owning.
That was unusual for him. These were the kinds of decisions I would have expected him to have thoughts about. But the conversation stayed with me because of how little he said.
A few weeks ago I finished a short reflection about Jonathan and his article, “Mourning the Future.” Then, this morning, I remembered that conversation.
For the first time, I wondered whether hearing about my future had been painful for him.

I was talking about where we might live and what our next chapter might look like. He was facing the knowledge that his own life was ending. Had I been asking him to picture a future he knew he wouldn’t be here to share?

I cannot know. I don’t want to put words into a silence he can no longer explain. He may have been tired. He may have had other things on his mind. Perhaps he was happy for us and sad for himself, feelings that could surely exist together.
But the possibility made me pause.

So much of retirement planning involves looking ahead. We consider whether to sell a house, where to live, and how to make our money last. Joey and I had been thinking about those questions as we imagined spending more of our lives in the Philippines.
There is an assumption beneath those conversations that we rarely say aloud: We expect to be here.

We know there are no guarantees. Yet when we make plans, we naturally picture ourselves living them: making the move, settling into a new home and going about our ordinary days. Joey and I were imagining that life together.
Jonathan was facing the loss of the years he had hoped were still ahead of him. What felt natural for me to talk about may have been painful for him to hear.

Looking back, I wish I had paused long enough to ask how he felt hearing about our plans. Not because I believe I should have hidden them from him. He was my brother, and sharing my life with him was natural. But perhaps there was room in that conversation for a question I didn’t think to ask.
What is it like for you when I talk about the years ahead?
I don’t know whether he would have wanted to answer. I wish I had given him the opportunity.

Grief brings back conversations we thought were finished. A few words, or the absence of them, acquire a meaning we didn’t recognize at the time. Sometimes that new meaning is an understanding. Sometimes it is only a question we will have to live with.

I am still looking forward to the life Joey and I hope to build. There is family to spend time with, a language to learn, and much to discover. Thinking about Jonathan does not take away my gratitude for those possibilities.
It does make me more aware of what it means to have them.
When I told him about our plans, I was thinking about a house we might sell and a country we might call home. Now I think about how much I would like to tell him what happens next.
And hear what he has to say.
